books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America
Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, C. Growing Tensions over Slavery

primary_sources: William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, 1831

stimulus.text: "On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. . . . I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD." — William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Wording checked against the first-edition text as reprinted by Britannica and the LibreTexts edition; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Garrison, The Liberator (1831)
stem: In 1831, a reader would have found Garrison's position most different from which earlier approach to ending slavery?

options.text: Quaker opposition to slavery on moral grounds
options.misconception: Quakers also called slavery wrong; they differed on tactics, not on the goal.

options.text: Free Black abolitionism, such as David Walker's Appeal
options.misconception: Walker also demanded an end to slavery now; Garrison learned from Black abolitionists.

options.text: Southern calls to defend slavery as a positive good
options.misconception: That defends slavery; it is not an approach to ending it.

options.text: Gradual emancipation paired with colonization in Africa

rationales.A: Quakers had opposed slavery for decades on moral grounds. Garrison shared their moral view and differed mainly in his louder, public tactics.
rationales.B: Walker's Appeal of 1829 urged Black people to resist slavery. Garrison was inspired by Walker, so the two stood close together.
rationales.C: Defending slavery as a positive good is the opposite of ending it. The question asks about approaches to ending slavery.
rationales.D: Before Garrison, most white antislavery groups favored freeing slaves slowly and sending freed people to Africa. Garrison broke with both ideas at once.
rationales.general:
1. List the old plan. Gradualists would free slaves slowly and colonize the freed in Africa.
2. List Garrison's plan. He demands freedom at once, with no payment and equal rights in America.
3. Compare the two. Every part of Garrison's demand breaks the old plan.
Background: The American Colonization Society, founded in 1817, sent about 12,000 African Americans to Liberia before the Civil War.
Remember: to see what is new, name the old plan first, then watch each part change.
